questions.question: Maya has 23 stickers. She puts them into groups of 4 stickers each. She fills 5 whole groups and some stickers are left over. What does the leftover number tell you?
options: 3 stickers are left over — not enough to make one more group of 4
23 ÷ 4 = 5 exactly, because leftover stickers do not count
7 stickers are left over, so 23 ÷ 4 = 4 R 7
Each group holds 3 stickers
questions.explain: Five groups of 4 use up 20 stickers, and 23 − 20 = 3, so the remainder 3 counts the stickers still waiting. The trap is saying 4 R 7: a leftover of 7 is bigger than the group size 4, so another whole group could still be made.

questions.question: A teacher has 30 markers and puts 7 markers into each cup. She fills 4 cups and 2 markers are left over. Why can the leftover never be 7 or more?
options: Because leftovers do not count, so the leftover is always 0
Because 7 or more markers would fill one more cup, so there would be 5 full cups instead of 4
Because the leftover always has to be bigger than 7
Because the leftover always equals the number of cups she filled
questions.explain: The remainder is what is left after you take out as many whole groups as you can, so it must be smaller than the group size — 7 leftover markers would just make another full cup. Watch out for answers that let the leftover be as big as or bigger than the number in each group.

questions.question: Liam has 26 hockey cards and shares them equally among 8 friends. Each friend gets the same whole number of cards, and any cards that are left stay with Liam. Which sentence matches what happens?
options: 26 ÷ 8 = 2 R 10, so each friend gets 2 cards and 10 stay with Liam
26 ÷ 8 = 3, so every card is handed out and none stay with Liam
26 ÷ 8 = 3 R 2, so each friend gets 3 cards and 2 stay with Liam
26 ÷ 8 = 2 R 3, so each friend gets 2 cards and 3 stay with Liam
questions.explain: Eight friends can each take 3 cards (8 × 3 = 24), and 26 − 24 = 2 cards stay with Liam. The 2 R 10 answer is a trap: 10 left over is more than 8 friends, so each friend could still take one more card.

questions.question: There are 45 students standing in equal rows of 6 students. Working it out gives 45 ÷ 6 = 7 R 3. What do the 7 and the 3 tell you?
options: 3 is the number of full rows, and 7 students are left standing
45 ÷ 6 = 6 R 9, so there are 6 full rows and 9 students left over
The 3 can be dropped, so 7 rows hold all 45 students
7 is the number of full rows of 6, and 3 students are left over with no full row
questions.explain: The quotient 7 counts the full rows (7 × 6 = 42) and the remainder 3 counts the students left over, since 45 − 42 = 3. Two traps here: swapping the quotient and the remainder, and leaving 9 left over when 9 is bigger than a row of 6.

questions.question: A whole number is divided by 9 and there is a remainder. What is the largest remainder that is possible?
options: 0, because remainders do not really count
questions.explain: A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor, so with a divisor of 9 the biggest it can be is 8. If the leftover reached 9, one more group of 9 would fit and the quotient would grow by 1.

questions.question: Aiden writes 137 ÷ 6 = 21 R 11. Without dividing again, how can you tell his answer is not finished?
options: It is fine, because 21 × 6 + 11 gives back 137
The remainder 11 is bigger than the divisor 6, so at least one more 6 still fits and the quotient should be larger
The remainder should just be dropped, so the answer is 21
The quotient 21 is bigger than the divisor 6, and that is not allowed
questions.explain: Multiplying back can look right and still be wrong: 21 × 6 + 11 = 137, but 11 leftover holds another whole 6, so the true answer is 22 R 5. Always check that the remainder is smaller than the divisor.

questions.question: A bakery packs 254 buns into boxes that hold 8 buns each. Working it out gives 254 ÷ 8 = 31 R 6. What does the 6 mean?
options: 254 ÷ 8 = 30 R 14, so 14 buns are left over
The 6 does not matter — the 31 boxes hold all 254 buns
6 buns are left over, which is not enough to fill another box of 8
There are 6 boxes still waiting to be packed
questions.explain: Thirty-one full boxes hold 31 × 8 = 248 buns, so 254 − 248 = 6 buns are left over and cannot fill a 32nd box. Saying 14 are left is a trap, because 14 buns would fill another box of 8 with 6 to spare.

questions.question: A skipping rope is 250 cm long. It is cut into pieces that are each 30 cm long. Working it out gives 250 ÷ 30 = 8 R 10. What does 8 R 10 mean for the rope?
options: 250 ÷ 30 = 7 R 40, so 7 pieces with 40 cm left over
8 full pieces of 30 cm, plus 10 more pieces
9 full pieces of 30 cm, because the last 10 cm counts as a piece
8 full pieces of 30 cm, with 10 cm of rope left that is too short to be another piece
questions.explain: Eight pieces use 8 × 30 = 240 cm, so 250 − 240 = 10 cm is left, and 10 cm is shorter than 30 cm so it cannot be a full piece. The trap is counting that short scrap as a whole piece, or leaving 40 cm over when 40 cm still holds another 30 cm piece.

questions.question: A Grade 5 class of 27 students is going to Stanley Park. Each van can carry 6 students. How many vans are needed so that every student gets a ride?
options: 5 vans — 4 vans are full and the last 3 students still need one more van
3 vans — 27 ÷ 6 = 3 R 9, so 3 full vans carry everyone
4 vans — 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3, and the 3 students left over are not counted
9 vans — because 27 ÷ 3 = 9, one van for every 3 students
questions.explain: 27 ÷ 6 = 4 R 3, and those 3 leftover students are real people who still need a ride, so one extra van is needed: 5 in all. The classic trap is stopping at 4 and leaving the remainder behind, or writing R 9 when 9 is bigger than the 6 seats in a van.

questions.question: Priya has $50 to spend on notebooks that cost $7 each. She buys as many as she can. How many notebooks does she get, and what does the leftover money mean?
options: 6 notebooks with $8 left, because 50 ÷ 7 = 6 R 8
7 notebooks, and the $1 left over stays in her pocket because it is not enough for another notebook
7 notebooks, and the leftover 1 means she needs only $1 more to buy another notebook
8 notebooks, because the money left over rounds up to one more notebook
questions.explain: Seven notebooks cost 7 × $7 = $49, so 50 ÷ 7 = 7 R 1 and the remainder is $1 of change she keeps. Here the leftover cannot be rounded up into another notebook, and $1 left does not mean $1 more is needed — she would need $6 more.

questions.question: A school orders 375 juice boxes and packs them into cases that hold 8 juice boxes each. Only completely full cases go to the gym; any juice box not in a full case is left in the staff room. How many juice boxes are left in the staff room?
options: 46, because that is how many cases go to the gym
0, because every juice box gets packed into a case somewhere
questions.explain: 375 ÷ 8 = 46 R 7, because 46 × 8 = 368 and 375 − 368 = 7, so the remainder 7 is the number of juice boxes left in the staff room. Do not answer with the quotient 46 — that counts cases, not juice boxes — and a remainder of 15 is impossible since 15 would fill another case of 8.

questions.question: For 178 ÷ 5 the answer is 35 R 3. In which situation should the final answer be written as 36 instead of 35 R 3?
options: Never — the remainder is always dropped, so 35 is the answer in every situation
When you write it as 35 R 5, because the remainder is allowed to equal the divisor
When the question asks how many tables are completely full
When the question asks how many tables seating 5 students are needed so all 178 students have a seat
questions.explain: 35 tables seat 5 × 35 = 175 students, and the 3 students left over still need somewhere to sit, so 36 tables are needed. The remainder is not always dropped and not always rounded up — you have to ask what the leftover means in the story, and it must always stay smaller than the divisor.
